function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

Below is a high‑level “recipe” for how I’d use the two tools you described to place a real‑world order for a burger and fries at McDonald’s.  
I’ll break it into logical phases, list the concrete actions I’d take with each tool, and note what I’d expect to see at each step.

---

## 1. Discover the McDonald’s Ordering API

| Tool | What I’d do | Why |
|------|-------------|-----|
| **Search tool** | *Query:* “McDonald’s online ordering API documentation” or “McDonald’s REST API for placing orders” | Find the official public or partner‑only API spec, or at least a developer portal that lists endpoints. |
| | *If the search returns a public endpoint* (e.g., `https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/orders`), capture the base URL and any required headers (e.g., `Authorization`, `X-Client-ID`). | These will be needed for subsequent calls. |
| | *If the search returns only internal or partner APIs*, note that I may need a partnership agreement or an OAuth flow to obtain a bearer token. | Without a valid token I can’t place an order. |

> **Outcome:** I now know the base URL, the path for creating an order (`POST /orders`), and any authentication mechanism (API key, OAuth, etc.).

---

## 2. Resolve Item Identifiers

| Tool | What I’d do | Why |
|------|-------------|-----|
| **Search tool** | *Query:* “McDonald’s menu API” or “McDonald’s product catalog” | Get the endpoint that lists available menu items (`GET /menu`) and the structure of the response. |
| | *If the API provides a catalog* (e.g., `GET https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/menu?location=...`), capture the URL and any query params (like `location`, `language`). | I’ll need to fetch the menu for my specific location to get accurate prices and availability. |
| | *If the API requires a location* (latitude/longitude), decide whether I’ll hard‑code a nearby McDonald’s or prompt the user for their address. | Location matters for delivery options, taxes, and menu variations. |

> **Outcome:** I now know how to fetch the menu and where to look for the IDs of “burger” and “fries”.

---

## 3. Gather User Context

| Tool | What I’d do | Why |
|------|-------------|-----|
| **Search tool** | *Query:* “McDonald’s delivery address validation API” | Some APIs require a validated address or ZIP code. |
| | *If the API exists* (e.g., `POST https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/validate-address`), capture the endpoint and expected payload. | I’ll validate the user’s address before attempting to place an order. |
| | *If no such API exists*, I’ll fall back to a generic geocoding service (Google Maps Geocoding API) to convert the address to lat/lng. | Needed for the menu request and for the order payload. |

> **Outcome:** I now have a validated address (or lat/lng) and a delivery window (if the API supports scheduling).

---

## 4. Authenticate (if required)

| Tool | What I’d do | Why |
|------|-------------|-----|
| **Search tool** | *Query:* “McDonald’s OAuth flow” | Determine whether I need to perform an OAuth dance (client credentials, authorization code, etc.). |
| | *If OAuth is required* (e.g., `POST https://auth.mcdonalds.com/token`), capture the token endpoint, grant types, and scopes. | I’ll need a bearer token for all subsequent calls. |
| | *If an API key suffices*, capture the key or the header name (`X-Api-Key`). | Simpler than OAuth but still needs secure storage. |

> **Outcome:** I now have a bearer token or API key ready to attach to every request.

---

## 5. Build the Order Payload

| Tool | What I’d do | Why |
|------|-------------|-----|
| **Execution tool** | *Construct a JSON payload* that includes:
| | • `items`: array of objects with `product_id` (from the menu lookup) and `quantity` (1 for each).
| | • `delivery_address`: the validated address or lat/lng.
| | • `payment_method`: e.g., `"card"` with a tokenized card reference (the user would have previously stored a card or I’d prompt them for a new one).
| | • `special_instructions`: optional (e.g., “no pickles”).
| | • `delivery_time`: optional (e.g., “now” or a scheduled slot).
| | • `customer_id`: optional (if the user has a loyalty account).
| | • `order_type`: `"delivery"` or `"pickup"`.
| | • `currency`: e.g., `"USD"`.
| | • `locale`: e.g., `"en-US"`.
| | • `tax_exempt`: optional (for corporate orders).
| | • `promo_code`: optional (if the user has a coupon).
| | • `customization`: e.g., “extra cheese” on the burger.
| | • `notes`: optional.
| | • `delivery_fee`: optional (some APIs let you override or request a quote first).
| | • `tip_amount`: optional (if the user wants to add a tip).
| | • `delivery_contact`: phone/email for the driver.
| | • `delivery_instructions`: e.g., “leave at door”.
| | • `delivery_location`: lat/lng for the driver’s navigation.
| | • `delivery_radius`: optional (to limit to a certain distance).
| | • `delivery_service`: e.g., “McDelivery”.
| | • `delivery_partner`: e.g., “Uber Eats” if integrated.
